passage: In Class 11 our school cricket team had a running joke about the boys from the Hill Road academy. We called them 'the cattle'. I, Dhruv, made up half the jokes: they moo instead of appealing, they need a farmer to set the field. It was easy to laugh, because they weren't really people to us, just a colour of jersey. Then at the district camp I was paired with Manoj from Hill Road for fielding drills. He was funny. He carried spare grips for everyone. On the last day he said, 'You're the one who does the cattle jokes, right? My little brother cried about that video.' I didn't know what to say. That's when I understood how the jokes had worked: as long as they had no faces, I didn't have to feel anything. I stopped making them. I still think about his brother.

Friday. During the snack break, Joseph (15) had the group laughing about the workers building the new flats next door: 'They're donkeys, na? Twenty of them in one room, can't even read a sign.' He made braying noises when one of them walked past the gate. Two younger boys copied him.

The bus stand in Barwani was hot and slow. Vikas held court on the bench.
“The harvest-labour families are back,” he said, jerking his chin toward a truck unloading bundles by the ginning mill. “Goats with phones. You can smell them from here.”
Uday laughed, because the others did. Vikas told another one, about how they “breed like cattle.” More laughs.
A girl from the truck, maybe fourteen like them, was helping an old woman down the step. She dropped a steel tumbler; it rolled toward the bench. Vikas pushed it back with his foot without looking up.
Uday picked it up instead and held it out. The girl said, “Thank you, bhaiya,” in careful Hindi.
Vikas snorted. But Uday felt something shift. The joke only worked if you didn't look at her face. He stopped laughing for the rest of the afternoon.

Every Friday, the lads from Fjell School crossed the bridge to use the Solberg pitch. And every Friday, Oskar had a new joke.
“Here come the hill trolls. Do they even speak, or just grunt?”
Xin smiled a little, not really amused. Oskar kept going: “They're like sheep. Follow the one with the ball.”
It got easier with every week. Oskar didn't know their names. He didn't want to.
This Friday, one of the Fjell boys went down hard on the concrete edge and didn't get up. Xin ran over. Oskar followed slowly.
The boy was holding his wrist, face white, trying not to cry in front of strangers. Xin knelt. “What's your name?”
“Emil.”
Oskar stood there. Emil. Not a troll, not a sheep. A fifteen-year-old whose hands were shaking. Oskar felt his face burn, then went to fetch the coach.

Dear Preeti,
I need to tell you something I'm ashamed of.
You know the jokes we always make about the Eastside school kids? "Eastside donkeys", the memes, the braying sounds when their bus passes. I've been sending them for a year. I thought it was harmless because they're not real to us. Just "them".
On Saturday I was at the inter-school quiz, and my partner from Eastside was a girl called Rukhsar. She knew every capital in Africa. She shared her water bottle when mine ran out. She told me her father drives a night bus and she studies on it.
On the way home I looked at our group chat and saw the donkey memes, and I felt sick. Rukhsar is one of the "donkeys".
I'm going to stop sending them. I hope you will too. I don't think we'd do it if we knew even one of them.
Vasudha
